clinicalPearls: Rare autosomal dominant glomerulopathy defined by massive accumulation of fibronectin within the mesangium and subendothelial space.
A substantial proportion of affected families carry heterozygous mutations in FN1, the gene encoding fibronectin, though many pedigrees remain genetically unexplained.
Usually presents in the second to fourth decades with proteinuria (which may reach nephrotic range), microscopic haematuria and hypertension.
Light microscopy shows enlarged, lobulated glomeruli with hyaline, strongly PAS-positive deposits and a membranoproliferative-like architecture.
Congo red staining is negative, a key feature distinguishing it from amyloidosis; the deposits stain positively for fibronectin.
Immunofluorescence for immunoglobulins and complement is typically negative or scant, underscoring the non-immune-complex nature of the disease.
Electron microscopy reveals granular to fibrillary electron-dense material expanding the mesangial and subendothelial regions.
Distal (type IV) renal tubular acidosis and disease recurrence in the transplanted kidney have both been reported.
reference.pathophysiology: Fibronectin glomerulopathy is a hereditary deposition disease characterised by the pathological accumulation of fibronectin, a large dimeric extracellular-matrix glycoprotein, within glomeruli. Inheritance is autosomal dominant, and heterozygous mutations in FN1 have been identified in a sizeable share of families, clustering in domains that mediate fibronectin self-assembly and heparin binding. Whether the deposited protein is chiefly plasma-derived (soluble circulating fibronectin) or locally synthesised has been debated, with much evidence favouring incorporation of plasma fibronectin into the glomerular matrix. The accumulating protein progressively expands the mesangium and subendothelial space, distorting glomerular architecture, narrowing capillary lumina and disrupting the filtration barrier to produce proteinuria and haematuria. Because the process is not driven by immune-complex deposition, immunofluorescence for immunoglobulins and complement is generally unremarkable, and the deposits are non-amyloid, remaining Congo red negative while staining strongly for fibronectin. Relentless matrix expansion leads to glomerular obliteration and slowly progressive loss of kidney function.
additionalDifferentials: Fibrillary glomerulonephritis (DNAJB9 positive, distinct fibril calibre)
additionalInvestigations: Renal biopsy with fibronectin immunostaining, Congo red and electron microscopy
FN1 genetic testing and pedigree/segregation analysis
DNAJB9 immunostaining to exclude fibrillary glomerulonephritis
Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with free light chains to exclude monoclonal disease
Quantification of proteinuria and serial kidney-function monitoring
Assessment for distal renal tubular acidosis where clinically suspected
Screening of at-risk relatives given dominant inheritance
redFlags: Progressive decline in kidney function towards kidney failure
Family members with unexplained kidney failure
Recurrence of proteinuria and deposits in a renal allograft
reference.prognosis: The disease is slowly progressive, with many affected individuals reaching kidney failure over years to decades; recurrence in the transplanted kidney has been described, so post-transplant surveillance is warranted.
pitfalls: Misclassifying the deposits as amyloid or as fibrillary glomerulonephritis without fibronectin and DNAJB9 staining
Omitting a dedicated fibronectin immunostain on biopsy
Overlooking the autosomal dominant family history and failing to counsel relatives
Mistaking the membranoproliferative-like pattern for an immune-complex glomerulonephritis
Attributing nodular glomerular changes to diabetes without confirmatory staining
